title: Democratizing Optimization with Generative AI
authors: David Simchi-Levi; Tinglong Dai; Ishai Menache; Michelle Xiao Wu
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States; Johns Hopkins University Carey Business School, Baltimore, Maryland, United States; Microsoft Research, Redmond, Washington, United States; Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, United States
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have captured the public imagination, whereas mathematical optimization remains little recognized beyond specialists. In this article, we argue that GenAI can bridge the persistent gap between optimization's technical capabilities and its limited real-world uptake. We present the 4I framework (Insight, Interpretability, Interactivity, Improvisation) as a set of design principles for combining GenAI with mathematical optimization. Insight establishes a trusted, up-to-date view of current operations; Interpretability explains model logic and trade-offs; Interactivity enables conversational what-if analysis; Improvisation supports model updates and event-driven re-optimization. By making optimization tools more intuitive, explainable, interactive, and adaptable, we envision a future in which frontline decision-makers can base their choices on rigorous, iterative analysis. We discuss how GenAI complements, rather than replaces, optimization: GenAI lowers barriers to modeling and interpretation; mathematical optimization reliably enforces the business goals, rules, and hard constraints encoded in the model. We also address emerging concerns, from hallucinations to the risk of over-reliance, and outline research directions for integrating GenAI and optimization responsibly. The GenAI boom gives the optimization community an opportunity to expand its impact by making optimization more accessible and trustworthy to a wider audience.

title: Rethinking Supplier Integration in Humanitarian Supply Chains: Feasibility and Constraints From an International Humanitarian Organization Perspective
authors: Jihee Kim; Nezih Altay; Stephen Pettit; Anthony Beresford
affiliations: School of Management Anglia Ruskin University Cambridge UK; Department of Management and Entrepreneurship DePaul University Chicago Illinois USA; Logistics and Operations Management Cardiff University Cardiff UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the widely recognized importance of integrative practices in commercial supply chain operations, their application in humanitarian supply chains (HSCs) remains underexplored. HSCs differ from commercial supply chains in their relational dynamics and integration processes, operating under extreme uncertainty, demand volatility, infrastructural disruption, and resource scarcity across a complex web of actors. Using an embedded single‐case design, this study assesses supplier integration (SI) in humanitarian operations in a leading international humanitarian organization (IHO), as well as the IHO's relationships with eight key suppliers. Drawing on the relational lenses of power, trust, and commitment, distinct integration patterns were identified across different supplier types. The findings highlight humanitarian‐specific contextual constraints and are used to inform a typology of SI feasibility encompassing feasible, selectively feasible, and low‐feasibility integration. This typology provides a foundation for guiding supplier relationship management in complex humanitarian contexts. This study offers a framework for understanding how relational and structural conditions shape integration in humanitarian settings and underscores the need for IHOs to adopt context‐appropriate supplier management approaches that reflect the unique dynamics of humanitarian operations.

title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
authors: Tiantian Yang; Jiayi Bao; Tianna Barnes; Ming D. Leung
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania; Texas A&M University; Dartmouth College; University of California, Irvine
abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that manipulates attire within candidates, using two photos of each candidate: one in professional attire, one in casual. The results converge across field and experimental data. Professional attire improves hiring prospects overall but yields substantially smaller returns for Black candidates. Moderated mediation tests confirm that perceived professionalism drives this disparity, such that race discounts how attire translates into perceived professionalism and how perceived professionalism translates into hiring. The racial gap attenuates in customer-facing roles in which appearance is task relevant. These findings challenge supply-side accounts of hiring inequality and reveal how a demand-side interpretation of equivalent signals perpetuates racial disadvantages.

title: Risk‐Oriented Differentiated Governance for Ambiguous Information
authors: Peikun Ni; Jianming Zhu; Hongzhou Zhang
affiliations: People's Public Security University of China Beijing China; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing China
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence has led to an exponential increase in false information, especially ambiguous information. Hampered by resource constraints, conventional governance approaches fall short of enabling efficient and precise risk management. In response, this paper innovatively proposes a risk‐oriented tiered governance framework tailored to ambiguous information. Specifically, we quantify epistemic uncertainty via multi‐level semantic features, combine it with network propagation features to determine latent influence scores, and construct a risk function capturing their synergy. Critical and acceptable boundaries are introduced to categorize ambiguous information into discrete risk levels, tier‐specific governance strategies are devised, and a propagation throttling (limiting each user's successful forwards per ambiguous information) strategy is innovatively proposed for medium‐risk information. Finally, we simulate differentiated governance strategies across risk levels of ambiguous information, systematically assess governance effectiveness, and offer a comparative discussion grounded in fairness and ethics. This study offers an operational analytical framework for refined risk governance of ambiguous information, contributes methodological innovations in risk quantification modeling and tiered governance strategies, and provides theoretical support and practical guidance for risk management authorities in designing differentiated measures.

title: The Aftermath of Almost: Communicating Risk Amid Community Narratives of Near Misses
authors: Elizabeth C. Ray; Anica Schramm; Patrick F. Merle
affiliations: School of Communication Florida State University Tallahassee Florida USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Unpredictable weather means that serious threats do not always unfold as forecast. Hurricane near misses create an especially challenging communication context: The absence of harm may invite community explanations that make the event feel less threatening, even as future risk persists. This study examines how community narratives and post‐event risk messages shape risk perception, collective efficacy, preparedness intentions, message sharing, and credibility after hurricane near misses. In an online experiment, Florida residents ( N = 405) viewed social media posts about a hurricane that shifted away from a coastal community. The posts varied by explanation type, comparing a symbolic community narrative with a factual account, and by response source, comparing emergency management, peer, and control messages. Results show limits and leverage points for post‐event risk communication: In the primary analysis, neither community narratives nor risk messages significantly shifted perceived risk; however, supplementary analyses accounting for regional residence revealed a small reduction in perceived risk following narrative exposure. Risk messages increased sharing and collective efficacy, and organizational sources were more credible than peer sources. These findings suggest that post‐event risk communication after near misses may not readily recalibrate individual risk perceptions but can shape how risk information circulates and how communities perceive their capacity to respond. The study advances understanding of near misses as ambiguous risk events in which communication matters even when harm does not occur.

title: Identification and Governance Strategy of Urban Systemic Risk Induced by Extreme Rain–Snow–Ice Weather in Southern China
authors: Wei Feng; Guirong Zhang
affiliations: School of Public Administration and Tourism Hunan University of Technology and Business Changsha Hunan P. R. China; School of Public Administration Central South University Changsha Hunan P. R. China; Center for Social Stability Risk Assessment Central South University Changsha Hunan P. R. China
abstract: ABSTRACT China's rapid urbanization has expanded urban spatial scale and increased the concentration of population, wealth, and infrastructure. Against the background of climate change, urban systemic risk induced by extreme rain–snow–ice weather (USR–RSI) in southern China has repeatedly disrupted critical infrastructure and public services, generating cascading impacts across interconnected urban systems. This study examines the generation and evolution of USR–RSI and develops a corresponding resilience governance strategy. Building on conceptual analysis, complex network theory and system vulnerability theory are integrated to construct the theoretical framework. A causal loop diagram is used to characterize risk diffusion and feedback mechanisms based on the 2008 and 2024 RSI disaster cases. Semi‐structured interviews and documentary materials are further analyzed using a structured data analysis approach to identify sensitivity and adaptive factors associated with node and path vulnerability. On the basis of these findings, a whole‐process resilience governance framework is proposed, covering resilience construction, integration of warning and response, rapid recovery, and long‐term adaptive optimization and transformative reconfiguration. The study provides an empirical and analytical basis for understanding and governing USR–RSI from the perspective of interconnected urban socio‐technical systems.

title: Hybrid Semi‐Quantitative Risk Assessment for Aging Offshore Platforms: A HAZOP–FMEA–Bow‐Tie Framework With Sensitivity Analysis and KRI‐Based Governance
authors: Muhammad Fawad Saleem; Majid Baseer; Qasim Tariq; Ahmad Khan
affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering University of Engineering and Technology, Peshawar 25120 Pakistan; Department of Engineering University of Palermo, Viale Delle Scienze, Building 9, 90133 Palermo Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT Aging offshore installations increasingly operate beyond their original design life, yet conventional periodic risk assessments capture barrier degradation only intermittently. This study presents a barrier‐conditioned semi‐quantitative risk‐assessment workflow that integrates Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), and bow‐tie barrier analysis. The workflow combines decomposed residual likelihood and consequence scoring with threshold‐stability testing and a Key Risk Indicator (KRI)‐based update rule. Its principal contribution is the governance linkage: an explicit rule set that maps barrier condition and KRI threshold breaches to changes in residual likelihood, residual consequence, and risk band between formal safety‐case reviews. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the workflow is demonstrated through a fully synthetic scenario representing a life‐extended semi‐submersible installation; all inputs are constructed and explicitly identified throughout as scenario assumptions. Under the illustrative scoring assumptions, a 19‐hazard register spanning seven hazard categories yields two high, nine medium, and eight low residual risks, with blowout/well‐control failure and hydrogen sulfide release remaining the highest residual risks. Per‐perturbation threshold‐stability analysis and distribution‐based Monte Carlo propagation indicate that 16 of the 19 residual risk ratings are sensitive to classification boundaries, suggesting that the reported scores should be interpreted as central estimates subject to uncertainty. The proposed workflow provides a transparent tool for risk screening and governance support, complementing full quantitative risk assessment (QRA) while preserving its essential analytical role.

title: The impact of geographical and technological proximity on knowledge spillovers from formal standards
authors: Peiyu Zhan; Silvia Massini; Mabel Sánchez-Barrioluengo
affiliations: Alliance Manchester Business School and Manchester Institute of Innovation Research, University of Manchester , Booth St W , Manchester M15 6PB,
abstract: Abstract Proximity is traditionally viewed as crucial for overcoming the search and transfer costs associated with imperfectly codified knowledge. But does proximity still matter when formal standard publication jointly enhances the codification, certainty, and accessibility of technical knowledge? Evidence from the U.S. Information and Communication Technology industry shows that technological proximity drives substantial spillover gains, largely irrespective of location. Conversely, geographical proximity confers a compensating advantage when technological proximity is low. We reveal a nuanced interplay of proximity in knowledge spillovers: while formal standardization effectively flattens the world for the technologically proximate, co-location remains vital for their less proximate counterparts.

title: Polycrisis and labour agency in global production networks: evidence from Bangladesh’s apparel industry
authors: Aysha Siddika
affiliations: Department of Social Science and Business, Roskilde University , Universitetsvej 1 , Roskilde 4000,
abstract: Abstract This article explains how temporally uneven polycrisis reshapes labour agency within apparel production networks. Developing a spatial–temporal analytical framework, it shows how interactions, amplification, and acceleration across crises reconfigure workers’ opportunity structures through legitimacy, profitability, and social reproduction pressures. This qualitative case study of Bangladesh’s apparel industry examines how the Rana Plaza accident, COVID-19, and the climate crisis interacted to produce cumulative effects that enabled openings and constrained mobilization, shifting labour agency across associational, coalitional, and micro-practices over time. The study advances labour regime analysis by demonstrating the temporal contingency and spatial situatedness of labour agency during polycrisis.

title: Toward an “Identity Turn” in Public Service Motivation Theory: A Problematizing Review and Research Agenda
authors: Lorenza Micacchi; Adrian Ritz
affiliations: University of Bern KPM Center for Public Management, , Schanzeneckstrasse 1, Bern,
abstract: Abstract Since its inception, Public Service Motivation (PSM) has been recognized as a key driver of behavior in public institutions. Despite its prominence, skepticism has emerged. In response, research has primarily focused on empirical analysis and measurement refinement rather than on conceptual development. This conceptual path dependency has become problematic as mixed empirical results increasingly challenge core theoretical propositions of PSM theory. We argue that one potential cause lies in a dominant assumption shaping the field: its positioning within motivation theory. To address this, we conducted a problematizing review across concepts and disciplines, comparing how PSM is understood in Public Administration with related concepts–such as motivation, altruism, and identity–in Management, Psychology, Sociology, and Economics. Based on this analysis, we propose a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes PSM as a social identity. In doing so, we outline a research agenda that (i) revises PSM’s core conceptual features and develops a new measurement approach informed by identity theory; (ii) introduces new ways of understanding PSM's functioning through identity work theory; and (iii) situates PSM theory within the broader debate on the “identity turn” in motivation research, highlighting its potential contribution to this multidisciplinary discourse.

title: EXPRESS: Customer-to-Manufacturer: Should a Platform Cooperate with More Manufacturers?
authors: Tonghuan Shi; Lin Tian; Zhen Xu
abstract: The traditional top-down relationship between manufacturers and consumers has led to persistently high failure rates in new product development. In response, the emerging customer-to-manufacturer (C2M) model leverages online platforms as intermediaries to directly transmit consumer feedback to manufacturers, thereby improving decision-making in product innovation and increasing the likelihood of product success. This paper develops an analytical model to study the strategic adoption of the C2M model in an online marketplace with one platform and two competing manufacturers. We focus on the role of platform information and examine how its trade-offs shape market outcomes. Our analysis shows that the impact of platform information on manufacturers' expected profits is non-monotonic. Moreover, manufacturers' cooperation decisions in C2M depend on the information price and are moderated by the amount of information. For the platform, unexpectedly, involving more manufacturers in C2M cooperation is not always optimal, especially when information is sufficient. We further show that the C2M model benefits the platform and consumers and improves social welfare, while potentially reducing manufacturers' profits. Overall, our results provide managerial and regulatory implications for platform-based C2M practices.

title: EXPRESS: Optimizing Size-Based Bundle Promotions: Balancing Customer Appeal and Product Costs
authors: Ruijiu Mao; Shuai Jia; Chung-Piaw Teo
abstract: Size-based bundle promotions (“ p -for- s ”) are widely used in retail to increase basket size, but designing them is challenging when product costs and customer preferences are heterogeneous. Customers favor high-value products; however, including such items increases the bundle’s cost and may require a higher price to sustain profitability. Existing models typically assume identical costs or uniform preferences and therefore largely overlook the interaction between cost heterogeneity and customer preferences. To examine this interaction, we begin with the “ p -for-1” case under classical MNL and mixed MNL models and provide clear structural insights: (i) cost heterogeneity makes assortment selection nontrivial, motivating joint optimization of assortment and pricing; (ii) preference heterogeneity makes optimization under mixed MNL models computationally difficult; and (iii) extending MNL to “ p -for- s ” settings requires approximations and becomes intractable as s grows. Building on these insights, we develop an optimization framework for general “ p -for- s ” promotions with multiple concurrent offers. Our approach uses sample average approximation (SAA) to approximate the valuation distribution with a finite sample of customer valuations and reformulates the resulting problem as a discrete bilevel program that captures surplus-maximizing customer behavior. To improve computational tractability, we combine the SAA-based mixed-integer reformulation with low-rank completion, customer clustering, and consideration-set construction. Finally, a large-scale case study using data from a major e-commerce retailer shows that our framework yields substantially higher model-implied profit than the cost-threshold heuristic and outperforms other bundle-promotion benchmarks.

title: EXPRESS: Partial or Full Doses First? Vaccine Allocation Under Limited Supply
authors: Ming Hu; Chaoyu Zhang; Yun Zhou
abstract: Vaccines have proven highly effective in curbing disease spread in the face of sudden large-scale infectious diseases. However, the challenge of limited vaccine supplies during initial mass production or in certain regions such as Africa poses a significant hurdle. To address this issue, one potential solution is the implementation of a fractional dosing approach, whereby individuals receive partial doses of the vaccine to achieve partial immunity. In this paper, we investigate the optimal vaccine allocation policy in scenarios where the vaccine supply is scarce. By exploring the trade-offs between administering fractional and full dosages, we formulate the problem as an optimal control problem under disease transmission dynamics to minimize the total number of infections over a planning horizon. Specifically, we extend the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model by introducing two new compartments for partially and fully vaccinated individuals. Under mild conditions, we demonstrate that an attainable optimal vaccine allocation policy exhibits a bang-bang structure, suggesting that either the Partial Doses First (PDF) or the Full Doses First (FDF) allocation policy achieves optimality at any time. Furthermore, we compare the committed PDF and FDF policies for the entire planning horizon and identify a critical threshold on the fractional-dose vaccine efficacy, such that when the efficacy is above (resp., below) this threshold, choosing the committed PDF (resp., FDF) policy is better. Using COVID-19 vaccination data, we calculate thresholds for different countries in January 2021 to recommend to governments whether the priority should be given to allocating the first dose or to prioritizing the allocation of both first and second doses to the population. We also illustrate the versatility of our proposed scarce capacity allocation model in addressing a broad spectrum of resource allocation problems under diffusion dynamics, for which partial resource allocation can still yield some, though not full, benefits and the optimal allocation decision involves balancing the coverage and protection level.

title: Buyer green innovation volatility and the supplier bullwhip effect: a signalling theory perspective
authors: Yan Hou; Shuili Yang; Lixu Li; Lujie Chen; Chenho Chao
affiliations: Xi’an University of Technology School of Economics and Management, , ,; Xi’an Jiaotong Liverpool University International Business School Suzhou, , ,; Emlyon Business School, Lyon, France
abstract: Purpose Buyers' green innovation does not remain confined within the firm; its volatility may ripple upstream and reshape suppliers' operations. Drawing on signalling theory, we examine how buyers' green innovation volatility (GIV) affects the supplier bullwhip effect (SBE), and how buyers' green supplier management (GSM) and inventory utilisation efficiency (IUE) moderate this effect. Design/methodology/approach We construct a dyadic dataset covering 436 Chinese buyer firms and 871 global suppliers from 2012 to 2022, and employ fixed-effects models to test our hypotheses. Findings There is a U-shaped GIV–SBE relationship: compared with both low and high levels of GIV, moderate GIV leads suppliers to adjust production more cautiously in response to unstable demand, resulting in lower SBE. When buyers' green innovation is on an overall downward trend, GSM helps suppliers interpret demand and operational changes more accurately, curbing GIV-induced increases in SBE. Higher IUE enables suppliers to detect GIV-related requirement changes more promptly, prompting stronger production responses and widening the SBE gap between moderate and low or high GIV. Originality/value By introducing GIV, our study identifies a novel antecedent of SBE and provides insights into how buyers can help suppliers accurately interpret GIV and calibrate their operational responses.

title: Making agentic AI explainable and auditable
authors: Gongtao Zhang; Jimmy Huang; Jonathan Seddon; Miao Wang
affiliations: University of Nottingham; Audencia Business School Departement Entrepreneuriat Strategie et Innovation; University of Nottingham Ningbo China
abstract: Agentic AI promises operational speed, yet in finance, opaque decision paths hinder regulatory auditability. We address this autonomy paradox with a knowledge-enabled explainability (KEE) design theory that makes compliance an intrinsic, explicitly governed system property. KEE decouples probabilistic learning from an explicit, rule-governed reasoning layer, relocating epistemic uncertainty from opaque model inference to a semantic structure that can be inspected, contested, and updated. This enables ante-hoc structural control through a semantic, programmable graph that encodes regulatory mandates as executable, inspectable constraints. The theory specifies three design principles: structural knowledge codification, topological reasoning scaffolding, and adaptive synchronization. It also introduces six guidelines that operationalize regulator-acceptable, path-based audit trails. A longitudinal study of a multinational fintech platform provides naturalistic evidence that KEE can support high-velocity operations while producing path-based audit trails and accommodating controlled changes to regulatory logic. The study contributes to design science by theorizing auditable autonomy as ante-hoc structural control, specifying the entity-concept-event paradigm as its ontological mechanism, and formalizing this mechanism as a prescriptive design theory for regulated agentic AI.

title: From Slack to Staff: Managers' Allocation of Slack Resources to Hiring
authors: Veroniek Collewaert; Ine Paeleman; Tom Vanacker; Frederik Anseel; Dries Bourgois
affiliations: Vlerick Business School; KU Leuven; University of Antwerp; Ghent University; University of Exeter; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
abstract: Abstract Prior research views cash holdings, or high‐discretionary slack, as a buffer against shocks or a catalyst for strategic change. Drawing on stakeholder salience theory, we argue that cash can also reshape managers' interpretation and prioritization of employee hiring‐related claims, thereby increasing hiring, and that this effect is more pronounced when structural influences heighten the salience of those claims. Study 1, a large‐scale field study of Belgian firms, finds a positive but diminishing relationship between cash and hiring. This relationship strengthens under conditions of greater firm dependence on specific employee groups or following an exogenous legal reform, both of which are hypothesized to make the salience of specific employee groups more apparent. In Study 2, a vignette experiment offers causal support for the hypothesized mechanism, with employee salience cues strengthening how managers translate cash into hiring allocations. Combined, our findings contribute to research on slack resources and stakeholder salience by showing that managers use high‐discretionary cash not only for buffering or strategic change but also to respond to salient stakeholders.

title: Beyond Leaderism: Recentering Leadership Science Towards Relationships in Action
authors: Janaki Gooty; Chou‐Yu (Joey) Tsai; Tiffany Keller Hansbrough; Peter D. Harms; Sean N. Walsh
affiliations: UNC Charlotte; Binghamton University; University of Alabama
abstract: Abstract The historical origins of ‘Great Man’ theories of leadership, and their contemporary offshoots, have produced an accumulated literature in which the leader's behaviours are the focal unit of analysis. This Point article surfaces five theoretical assumptions underlying the leader behavioural paradigm: leaderism, individualistic attribution, behavioural universalism, democratization of leadership, and individual‐level ontology. We discuss theoretical counterfactuals to each assumption and call for a shift in the scene of scholarly conversation, from individual leaders to relationships that incorporate context and stakeholders. This shift in the focal unit of analysis from individual leader behaviour to relationships represents a foundational theoretical pivot built on multidisciplinary foundations, attention to levels of analysis, and a deep grounding in context. By questioning the assumptions underlying 85 years of leader behaviour research, we argue that the science (episteme), skill development (techné), and contextual judgement (phronesis) of leadership could be more tightly coupled by directing the spotlight towards relationships in context rather than individual leaders. In doing so, we move the focus from leaders in action to leadership as relationships in action .

title: Accounting Comparability and Common Owners
authors: Maimuna Akter; Justin Chircop; Douglas Cumming; Monika Tarsalewska
affiliations: School of Business Administration Gonzaga University 502 E Boone Ave Spokane WA 99258 USA; Lancaster University Management School Lancaster University Lancaster LA1 4YX UK; Professor of Finance and Steven Shulman ’62 Endowed Chair of Digital Innovation, Stevens Institute of Technology School of Business 1 Castle Point Terrace Hoboken NJ 07030 USA; University of Exeter Business School Streatham Court, Streatham Campus Rennes Drive Exeter EX4 4PU UK; Kozminski University 57/59 Jagiellonska Street Warsaw 03–301 Poland
abstract: Abstract We examine the relationship between accounting comparability and common ownership. Accounting comparability can reduce information asymmetry between firms and investors by lowering information acquisition and processing costs. At the same time, greater comparability can reduce the private information advantages that sophisticated investors, such as common owners, exploit. Which of these opposing forces dominates is ultimately an empirical question. Using a sample of US firms for 1999–2021, we find that accounting comparability is positively associated with common ownership, particularly non‐transient common ownership. Further analyses indicate that this relation is driven by a reduction in information asymmetry and is significantly stronger among firms with weaker information environments.

Belief in mean reversion and the law of small numbers
authors: Jawwad Noor; Fernando Payró
affiliations: Department of Economics, Boston University; Department of Economics and Economic History, Universitat Autónoma de Barcelona; Barcelona School of Economics
abstract: Studies find that people systematically underestimate the likelihood of streaks in a random sequence. In a canonical coin‐tossing environment, this paper shows that the evidence can be explained by a belief in mean reversion. Such beliefs are represented as if the bias of the coin is history‐dependent and “self‐correcting.” In a Bayesian inference setting, a belief in mean reversion ensures that the agent never rules out the true parameter.

title: Information design in smooth games
authors: Alex Smolin; Takuro Yamashita
affiliations: Department of Economics, Toulouse School of Economics; Institute of Social and Economic Research, Osaka University
abstract: We study information design in games where players choose from a continuum of actions and have continuously differentiable payoffs. We show that an information structure is optimal when the equilibrium it induces can also be implemented in a principal–agent contracting problem. Building on this result, we characterize optimal information structures in symmetric linear‐quadratic games. With common values, targeted disclosure is robustly optimal across all priors. With interdependent and normally distributed values, linear disclosure is uniquely optimal. We illustrate our findings with applications in venture capital, Bayesian polarization, and price competition.

title: Combinator dynamics: Multidimensional evolutionary learning
authors: Srinivas Arigapudi; Omer Edhan; Yuval Heller; Ziv Hellman
affiliations: Department of Economic Sciences, IIT Kanpur; Department of Economics, University of Manchester; Department of Economics, Bar-Ilan University
abstract: In complex strategic settings with multiple dimensions, players often simplify decisions by breaking them down into separate dimensions. In contrast to standard replicator dynamics, which assume perfect multidimensional coordination, our combinator dynamics model captures cases in which players revise actions dimension by dimension, imitate successful traits in each dimension, and then combine the selected traits into a new action. We analyze key properties of these dynamics—monotonicity, stationarity, and stability. We then extend the model to heterogeneous settings, where some players imitate entire multidimensional actions while others combine traits imitated separately in each dimension. We apply the framework to organizational decision‐making, where decentralized adoption of practices can generate coordination failures, persistent performance differences, and a trade‐off between specialized and versatile organizational traits.

title: Contract terms monotonicity in matching markets
authors: Cyril Rouault
affiliations: CEPS, ENS Paris-Saclay, University of Paris-Saclay
abstract: We study doctor–hospital matching markets with contracts, in which hospitals can offer a range of contract terms to doctors. We show that introducing new terms can reduce doctors' welfare, whereas withdrawing terms may generate a Pareto improvement. We establish the preference domains under which welfare is preserved and show that only agent‐lexicographic preferences for all agents ensure that no doctor is worse off when additional terms are introduced. Since this condition is rarely satisfied in practice, our results imply that most real‐world markets are vulnerable to welfare losses when the set of contract terms expands.

title: Optimal auction design with contingent payments and costly verification
authors: Ian Ball; Teemu Pekkarinen
affiliations: Department of Economics, MIT; Department of Economics, University of Vaasa
abstract: We study the design of an auction for an income‐generating asset such as an intellectual property license. Each bidder has a signal about his future income from acquiring the asset. After the asset is allocated, the winner's income from the asset is realized privately. The principal can audit the winner, at a cost, and then charge a payment contingent on the winner's realized income. We solve for an auction that maximizes the principal's revenue, net of auditing costs. The winning bidder is charged linear royalties up to a cap, beyond which there is no auditing. A higher bidder pays more in cash upfront and faces a lower royalty cap.

title: Semistability in roommate problems
authors: P. Jean-Jacques Herings; Yu Zhou
affiliations: Department of Econometrics and Operations Research, Tilburg University; College of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology; Graduate School of Economics, Nagoya University
abstract: We study the roommate problem allowing for preferences with indifferences and agents remaining single. A stable outcome need not exist. We introduce semi‐stability, a novel notion that guarantees existence and restores stability through minimal policy or group interventions. We build an equilibrium foundation for semistability by showing its equivalence to a newly proposed choice‐based equilibrium concept. We show that undominated semistable outcomes are Pareto optimal and under strict preferences, every semistable outcome is Pareto optimal. Nevertheless, standard structural properties, such as the rural hospital theorem and the lattice properties, fail for semistable outcomes. We also discuss possible applications.

title: Selling information for bilateral trade
authors: Robert Evans; In-Uck Park
affiliations: Faculty of Economics, University of Cambridge; School of Economics, University of Bristol
abstract: We study the design and pricing of information by independent information providers for a buyer engaged in a trading relationship with a seller, and examine their welfare implications. While competitive information firms would sell full information about the value of the good, a monopolist supplies limited information in a particularly simple form—often resulting in higher total surplus than under full information, by influencing the seller's pricing decision. If only a single information structure can be offered, it takes a binary threshold form. If the provider can offer a menu of priced information structures before the seller sets a price, he offers a continuum of thresholds, inducing a unit‐elastic demand function for the seller. In both scenarios, the information firm increases total welfare when the seller's production cost is high but reduces it when the cost is low.

title: Collaboration between and within groups
authors: Matias Iaryczower; Santiago Oliveros; Parth Parihar
affiliations: Department of Politics, Princeton University; Department of Economics, University of Bristol; Center of Excellence for Negotiations and Analytics, BASF
abstract: We study the ability of multigroup teams to undertake binary projects in a decentralized environment. The equilibrium outcomes of our model display familiar features in collaborative settings, including inefficient gradualism, inaction, and contribution cycles, wherein groups alternate taking responsibility for moving the project forward. Expected delay grows more than proportionally with project size, and some welfare‐enhancing projects are not completed, even as agents become arbitrarily patient. A team composed of two equally large groups can complete larger projects than a fully homogeneous team, even as the difference in preferences for completion among the two groups is arbitrarily small. Moreover, if the project is sufficiently large, the two‐group team always completes the project strictly faster.

title: Informed communication equilibrium
authors: Frédéric Koessler; Vasiliki Skreta
affiliations: GREGHEC, HEC Paris – CNRS; UCL, UT Austin; CEPR
abstract: We consider a privately informed principal selecting a communication device to influence players' actions. In contrast to standard information design, the principal cannot commit ex ante, and the device must elicit information from all players. We define an informed communication equilibrium (informed CE) as a perfect Bayesian equilibrium outcome of this informed communication design game. We show that the set of informed CE is the subset of communication equilibria (CE) that yield principal payoff vectors bounded below by an equilibrium payoff vector of the silent game, under some consistent interim beliefs. The ex ante optimal CE may fail to be an informed CE. We provide sufficient conditions for a CE to be an informed CE and identify classes of games in which CE and informed CE coincide.

title: Repeated games with many players
authors: Takuo Sugaya; Alexander Wolitzky
affiliations: Graduate School of Business, Stanford University; Department of Economics, MIT
abstract: Motivated by the problem of sustaining cooperation in large groups with limited information, we analyze the relationship between group size, monitoring precision, and discounting in repeated games with independent, player‐level noise. The viability of cooperation under independent noise is linked to the per‐capita channel capacity of the stage‐game monitoring structure. We show that cooperation is impossible if the per‐capita channel capacity is much smaller than the discount rate. A folk theorem under a novel identification condition provides a near converse. If attention is restricted to co‐linear equilibria (a generalization of strongly symmetric equilibria), cooperation is possible only under much more severe parameter restrictions.

title: Strategic experimentation with privately observed payoffs
authors: Jérôme Renault; Eilon Solan; Nicolas Vieille
affiliations: Mathematics and Statistics Department, Toulouse School of Economics, Université Toulouse Capitole; School of Mathematical Sciences, Tel Aviv University; Department of Economics and Decision Sciences, HEC Paris
abstract: We study a strategic experimentation game with exponential bandits in which experiment outcomes are private. The equilibrium amount of experimentation is always weakly higher than with public outcomes. Moreover, in pure equilibria, experimentation is never significantly below the socially optimal level and may be strictly higher. We provide a tight bound on the extent of over‐experimentation. The analysis rests on a novel encouragement effect.

title: Life‐Cycle Wage Growth and Firm Productivity in Developed and Developing Economies
authors: Kerstin Holzheu; Juan Munoz‐Morales
affiliations: Sciences Po (CNRS) & IZA & CESifo; Univ. Lille, CNRS, IESEG School of Management, UMR 9221 ‐ LEM ‐ Lille Économie Management Lille F‐59000 France
abstract: ABSTRACT Life‐cycle wage growth varies substantially across countries. We study the firm productivity distribution's role in a random‐search model with learning and labor‐market frictions, estimated for Brazil, Colombia, and the United States. Brazil has a long left tail of low‐paying firms, and Colombia has a highly compressed firm ladder. Replacing each country's firm distribution with that of the United States closes most of the cross‐country gap in wage growth, raising Brazil's relative wage growth from 73 to 103 percent and Colombia's from 52 to 115 percent. The results are robust to alternative distributional assumptions and additional sensitivity checks.

title: ASYMPTOTIC PROPERTIES OF APPROXIMATE MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATOR IN MARKOV-SWITCHING STATE-SPACE MODELS
authors: Chaojun Li
affiliations: East China Normal University
abstract: For Markov-switching state-space models, it is practically infeasible to compute the likelihood function through the Kalman filter because of the path dependence on regimes. A widely applied approximation algorithm uses a collapsing step to average out the most dated regime and truncates the regime path. This algorithm’s performance, however, has not been examined analytically. This study fills the gap. We characterize the parameters that affect the approximation error, derive the upper bounds of the errors in likelihood computation and latent variable inference, and investigate the asymptotic properties of the approximate maximum likelihood estimator. We also provide a practical procedure for measuring approximation errors and selecting the number of regime periods to keep in the truncated path. All the analysis is based on our new collapsing step, which removes a nonlinear adjustment term in the existing method to facilitate theoretical derivations.

title: Marebito: citation matching interface for the digital library zbMATH open
authors: Madhurima Deb; Isabel Beckenbach; Norman Meuschke; Olaf Teschke; Moritz Schubotz
abstract: Abstract zbMATH Open is a leading curated bibliographic database covering approximately five million publications in mathematics. This paper presents Marebito, a production citation-matching system developed for zbMATH Open, and documents its architecture, domain-adapted feature design, and operational performance at scale. Marebito combines bibliographic parsing with GROBID, candidate retrieval with Elasticsearch, and a supervised Random Forest trained on domain-specific string-similarity features. Evaluation on internal zbMATH Open datasets yields precision and recall exceeding 98% on modern DOI-indexed records. Evaluation across two bibliographically distinct subsets reveals that classifier performance is strongly conditioned on metadata completeness, particularly title and author string quality, rather than DOI availability alone, documenting a concrete challenge for citation matching in mathematical literature. A preliminary comparison with Crossref on a manually verified subset of 2,037 entries illustrates the limitations of general-purpose matchers on specialist mathematical bibliography. A neural reranking baseline confirms that Elasticsearch-derived hard negatives are essential for abstention. We also discuss downstream bibliometric applications within zbMATH Open.

title: Pursuing transparency: how research organizations in Germany collect data on publication costs
authors: Dorothea Strecker; Heinz Pampel; Jonas Höfting
affiliations: IBI, HU Berlin; OS Office, Helmholtz
abstract: Abstract This article presents the results of a survey conducted in 2024 among research performing organizations (RPOs) in Germany on how they collect data on publication costs. Of the 583 invitees, 258 (44.3%) completed the questionnaire. This survey is the first comprehensive study on the recording of publication costs at RPOs in Germany. The results show that the majority of surveyed RPOs recorded publication costs at least in part. However, procedures in this regard were often non-binding. Respondents’ ratings of the reliability of the collection of data on publication costs varied by the source of publication funding. Eighty percent of respondents rated the contribution of collecting data on publication costs to shaping the open access transformation as “very important” or “important.” Yet, these data were used as a basis for strategic decisions in only 59% of the surveyed RPOs. Moreover, most respondents considered the implementation of an information budget at their institutions by 2025 unlikely. We discuss the implications of these findings for the open access transformation.

title: Survivors in science: A comprehensive analysis of gender disparities
authors: Marek Kwiek; Lukasz Szymula
affiliations: Center for Public Policy Studies (CPPS), Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznan, Poland; Department of Artificial Intelligence, Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznan, Poland
abstract: Abstract Gender inequality in scientific careers can emerge at two analytically distinct margins: inequality in who remains in science and inequality among those who remain. While the former has been examined in research on attrition in science, much less is known about gender disparities among scientists who remain active for a long period. We address this gap by following “survivors in science”—scientists who started publishing in 2000 and continued publishing until 2020–2023 (N = 41,424). Together, they authored more than 2 million publications (N = 2,089,097) containing over 70 million cited references (N = 73,118,395) and worked in 38 OECD countries. Using raw Scopus data, we examine gender disparities in publishing intensity, international collaboration, journal prestige, productivity, citation impact and team size. Our findings reveal that men were on average 23% more productive than women cumulatively in 2000–2023 and 19% more productive in 2019–2023. By contrast, women and men published in similarly prestigious journals, achieved similar field-normalized citation impact, and worked in similarly sized teams. The structure of gender inequality is career-stage dependent: Disparities observed in broader populations of scientists need not persist among those who remain active in science longer, while the gender productivity gap persists.

title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
authors: FERHAT AKBAS; MINJIE HUANG; FELIX MESCHKE
abstract: ABSTRACT We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects
authors: Cláudia Custódio; Miguel A. Ferreira; Emilia Garcia-Appendini; Adrian Lam
affiliations: Imperial College Business School; Nova School of Business and Economics; University of St. Gallen; University of Pittsburgh
abstract: Abstract We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.
journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?
authors: Cloé Garnache
affiliations: Oslo Metropolitan University Housing Lab and Center for Energy Policy and Economics (CEPE), ETH Zürich
abstract: Abstract Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.

title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
authors: Ilias Filippou; David E. Rapach; Mark P. Taylor; Guofu Zhou
affiliations: Florida State University; Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta; Washington University in St. Louis and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR); Washington University in St. Louis
abstract: Abstract The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.
journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Housing Yields
authors: Stefano Colonnello; Roberto Marfè; Qizhou Xiong
affiliations: Ca’ Foscari University of Venice; University of Turin, and Collegio Carlo Alberto; University of Oxford
abstract: Abstract We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.

title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
authors: Nathan Lassance; Alberto Martín-Utrera
affiliations: LFIN/LIDAM, UCLouvain; Iowa State University
abstract: Abstract We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. JEL Classification: G11, G12.

title:
Demand‐Driven Propagation of Job Losses: Evidence from the Great Recession
                    <sup>a</sup>
authors: HA NGUYEN; JIAMING SOH
abstract: Abstract This paper presents evidence for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses in the context of the United States during the Great Recession. Using county‐level tradable job losses driven by aggregate shocks as an instrument, it shows that retail and restaurant (R&R) employment fell by 0.37% for every 1% of job loss in the rest of the county's economy. The finding is not driven by the house price decline or by credit supply problems. Moreover, the spillover is more severe for R&R industries that are most affected by consumer demand shocks during the Great Recession, which strengthens the argument for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses.

title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
authors: Miao Liu; Wanrong Xu; Rachel Xi Zhang
affiliations: Boston College; Southern University of Science and Technology; National University of Singapore
abstract: ABSTRACT Although extensive research examines the costs and benefits of adopting new disclosure regulations, little addresses the consequences of regulatory inaction. We investigate whether firms in nonadopting countries incur additional information losses, beyond the forgone benefits, when their foreign peers adopt International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Nonadopters bear an absolute liquidity cost as foreign peers adopt IFRS, consistent with negative externalities from IFRS and accompanying reforms. Exploiting heterogeneity across nonadopting countries, we observe more pronounced liquidity declines among firms with greater institutional ownership overlap with IFRS peers. This effect appears more pronounced when IFRS peers are domiciled in countries with concurrent enforcement reforms or greater comparability improvements. Further evidence shows shared intermediaries—investors and analysts—reduce information production for nonadopters as other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Overall, regulatory inaction degrades information environments: resources shift to the new regime, worsening liquidity for firms in the old regime. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from commercial sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G1; K22; M41; M48.

title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
authors: James J. Blann; Phillip T. Lamoreaux; Beverly J. Larson
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology; Arizona State University; University of Florida
abstract: ABSTRACT Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; M48; F21; L51; G15; G18.

title: Music divisions and cultural hierarchy in China: how transnational, political, and historical forces shape symbolic boundaries
authors: Gordon C Li
affiliations: Rikkyo University , 3-34-1 Nishi-Ikebukuro, Toshima-ku, Tokyo 171-8501 ,; National Taipei University of Technology , 1, Sec. 3, Zhongxiao E. Rd., Taipei 10608 ,
abstract: Abstract This study maps the division of music in China and examines the mechanisms underlying its formation. Methodologically, it introduces multidimensional item response theory (MIRT), a latent-trait approach rarely used in cultural sociology, to identify the social divisions of taste before examining their social stratification through regression analysis. The findings reveal six taste profiles: high-status traditional music; pop music stratified into middlebrow Hong Kong and Taiwan classics, unstratified mainstream Chinese pop, and low-status local music; and foreign music divided into high-status selective forms and unstratified trendy foreign pop. These divisions do not cleanly align with genre categories, a highbrow–lowbrow hierarchy, or omnivore–univore patterns in established accounts. Instead, they reveal dual forms of high-status taste—state-consecrated heritage and cosmopolitan selective foreign pop—reflecting a multidimensional structure organized around region of origin, historical prestige, cohort, and popularity. More broadly, this study reveals how cultural stratification in China extends beyond Bourdieusian models centered on domestic field competition to encompass global flows, state-directed legitimation, and historical local trajectories. These findings extend theories of cultural distinction beyond the assumptions derived from dominant Western liberal-market societies and offer a framework for understanding how cultural hierarchies are constituted across wider national contexts.

title: Workplace authority in China: gender, parenthood, and work sectors
authors: Manlin Cai
affiliations: Department of Sociology, The University of British Columbia , 2011 West Mall, Vancouver, BC V6T 1Z2 ,
abstract: Abstract Workplace authority is a key individual and organizational resource to which women typically have more limited access than men. Yet, less is known about how parenthood shapes this gender disparity and how the relationship varies across employment regimes. Drawing on nationally representative, longitudinal data from the China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022), I examine within-person changes in women’s and men’s access to supervisory authority following parenthood, with particular attention to variation across the state and private sectors. Fixed-effects results show that, overall, women’s likelihood of holding authority declines after becoming mothers, especially after having two or more children, whereas men experience little change. These dynamics differ by work sector. A considerable motherhood penalty is concentrated in the private sector, whereas a fatherhood premium emerges only in the state sector. Parenthood therefore widens the gender gap in authority in both sectors through distinct patterns. These findings suggest that employment regimes condition the gendered meanings of parenthood and how they translate into access to authority. In China, the state sector’s formal protections may buffer motherhood-related disadvantages, whereas its male-dominated hierarchy and pronatalist agendas may sustain fatherhood-related rewards.

title: Women and the double standard of ambition
authors: Geertje J. Bol
affiliations: History Department University of Fribourg Fribourg Switzerland
abstract: Abstract Few human qualities are as morally unstable as ambition: We seem unable to decide whether to admire or condemn the desire for self‐advancement. This instability guarantees double standards—and none has been more enduring than that of women's ambition. This article traces the emergence of this double standard in early modern England, when ambition came to be widely accepted as natural and even virtuous in men, yet remained unnatural and vicious in women. It then turns to four seventeenth‐century feminists—Rachel Speght, Margaret Cavendish, Mary Astell, and Judith Drake—who challenged this emerging double standard. They reimagined ambition as a feminist tool, using it to argue for women's equality and even superiority. Unearthing this neglected strand of ambitious feminism not only contributes to the history of political thought but also points the way to a reconciliation between feminism and ambition that avoids the pitfalls identified by feminist theorists today.

title: Can citizen election observation increase public confidence in US elections?
authors: Jennie Barker; Oren Samet; Susan D. Hyde
affiliations: SNF Agora Academy Postdoctoral Fellow, SNF Agora Institute Johns Hopkins University Baltimore Maryland USA; Assistant Professor, Department of Political Science Rice University Houston Texas USA; Robson Professor, Department of Political Science University of California Berkeley California USA
abstract: Abstract Nonpartisan citizen election observation plays an important role in promoting the credibility of electoral processes around the world. This article assesses whether nonpartisan observation can shape attitudes among the US public, randomizing information about nonpartisan domestic observers in a series of survey experiments fielded to nearly 10,000 respondents. These included both hypothetical vignettes and information about a real‐world nonpartisan domestic observation mission undertaken by The Carter Center during the 2022 midterm elections in Fulton County, Georgia. The results show that information about positive assessments by nonpartisan observers of the hypothetical and Fulton County elections increased respondents' confidence in electoral results and processes, and also made respondents more likely to identify the officially announced winner over the candidate they favored as the candidate who won. Alternative ways of framing observers were largely inconsequential.

title: How does Coethnicity with Refugees Shape their Reception? Evidence from Afghan Refugees in Pakistan
authors: Mashail Malik; Niloufer Siddiqui; Yang-Yang Zhou
